title: not a building
hookLine: not a building — the people; the Greek word means "the called-out ones"
tomorrow: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead

lines: "THE CHURCH THAT IS IN THEIR HOUSE."
cards: Say the word church and a picture comes up. A steeple. Stained glass.

A cathedral so big your voice echoes, or a strip-mall storefront with folding chairs. Everybody pictures a building. But for about the first two hundred years, Christians had almost no church buildings at all.

They met in kitchens and courtyards, around somebody's table. Paul ends one of his letters with greetings to a married couple, and adds: "greet the church that is in their house." The church was in the house.
Which means it wasn't the house.

teach.b: The word in the New Testament is Greek: ekklesia. It's made of two small pieces: ek, out, and a word for calling. The called-out ones.
In a Greek city, the ekklesia was the assembly: the citizens called out of their homes to gather and decide things together. It wasn't a place. It was people, showing up.
So when the first Christians needed a word for themselves, that's the one they picked. Not the temple. Not a sacred site.
The gathering. Paul pushes it further.
He tells one of his churches: "ye are the body of Christ." Hands, feet, eyes, ears. All different.

None of them the whole thing, and none able to say to the others, I don't need you. That's how he pictures a church: not a crowd of the same person, but a body of very different ones. Then the smallest church there is.
In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus promises: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Two or three. Not two or three hundred.
Christians today gather in every size there is. Cathedrals that took centuries to build. House churches still meeting around a kitchen table.
A hospital room, a prison, a video call. Churches differ a lot about how they're led and how they're joined. But almost all of them would say this much: the building is where the church meets.
The people are the church. Which is why it can hurt so much when they fail you. If a church once hurt you, that's real, and it isn't small.
Many Christians would say the people who failed you aren't the whole church, and they aren't Christ.

how: Many Christians gather with a church on Sundays for worship, and many also meet in small groups at home during the week. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches are organized differently, but all speak of the church as the people, not the building.

games.q: you're one of the first Christians, about the year 60. it's the Lord's day. where do you go to meet the church?
o: a believer's house, around their table.
games.why: a house. there were almost no church buildings yet. the church met in homes, and Paul greeted "the church that is in their house."

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe out slowly. Think of the two or three people you'd call if something went wrong tonight.
The ones who'd show up. Picture them, one at a time: their faces, where they are right now. Then widen it a little, to someone who showed up for you once and never knew what it meant.
If you pray, you can gather them in your prayer. If you don't, just let them be gathered here with you for a minute.

wordCard.voice: The church. Ekklesia. Not a building: the called-out ones, gathered. Twentieth word.

orig.note: Greek. ek (out) + a word for calling: the assembly, the called-out ones. the New Testament's word for church.

carryVoice: Your line: find two or three. That's the smallest church there is, and it counts. Day twenty.
